display_name: Plantagenet Omrah Pinot Noir, Great Southern
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "2011 was a cool, late harvest in Great Southern, and Omrah Pinot carries that tension in its bones: bright red cherry riding on wet granite acidity, no new oak to hide the lateritic iron snap. A bronze medal at TEXSOM is the only critic stamp that exists, which keeps the price sane and the vineyard story front-and-center.",
  "wine_summary": "Plantagenet, founded 1968, was the first winery to bottle under the Mount Barker sub-region name; Omrah is its early-drink label, built from estate and grower blocks across the wider Great Southern GI. 2011 delivered small berries and high malic acid—winemakers let the fruit speak, keeping cask age neutral so the wine reads as alpine-Pinot rather than small-barrel spice. The result is a regional snapshot: gravelly iron laterites pushing snap-pea sap and cranberry, maritime breeze (Albany 30 km away) tightening the finish to sashimi-grade acidity.",
  "terroir_expression": "Great Southern sits on 1.1-billion-year-old gneiss and granite; the Omrah blocks lie on lateritic gravelly sandy loams shot through with ironstone. That iron gives the palate a hematite tug—think licking a cold river stone—while the granite sand drains quickly, stressing canopies and concentrating skin phenolics. Morning fog off the Southern Ocean rolls 30 km inland, extending hang time and locking in malic acid that translates to crunchy red apple on the palate.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fruit is destemmed, cold-soaked 3 days, then fermented in small open stainless lots with daily punch-downs kept under 28 °C to preserve volatile cherry esters; 20 % whole clusters add stem-tannin snap. Maturation is ten months in 3- to 6-year-old French hogsheads—large 300 L barrels that soften acidity through micro-oxidation without adding oak lactones—then bottled with a light pad filtration at 12.5 % ABV.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot chicken on white bread—the wine’s acid and light tannin scrub the cayenne oil and refresh between bites.",
    "Cold soba with soy-poached shiitake and sesame—granitic iron notes echo the mushroom earth while tart cranberry lifts the soy.",
    "Tea-smoked duck breast, plum skin on—ironstone minerality mirrors the game, low oak lets the plum fruit sing.",
    "Fine-dining: grilled pink ling with smoked-eel beurre blanc—oceanic salinity in both wine and sauce, Pinot red-fruit bridges the beurre."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Stargazer Pinot Noir, Tasmania — similar cool-year acidity and whole-cluster snap, priced $5-10 higher.",
    "Fleurie ‘Les Moriers’ from Chignard — granite tannin and tart cherry parallel, but Beaujolais cru gives softer mid-palate.",
    "Oregon A to Z Pinot — same early-drink, neutral-oak ethos, though Oregon delivers darker fruit and less iron-mineral edge."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Light-bodied dry red with high acidity and iron-mineral crunch",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 2026 for crunchy fruit; decade-old vintages of Omrah show leather but lose lift, so don’t cellar longer than five years. Store at 13 °C, screw-cap keeps ullage risk near zero.",
  "value_assessment": "$22–26 retail in Australia, often $18 on deal. At that money it competes with Yarra’s Coldstream Hills and Marlborough’s Mount Difficulty, both $30+. You get regional iron-granite clarity for entry-pinot dollars, making it a weekday no-brainer.",
  "market_position": "You’ll spot Omrah限时特价 shelves at Dan Murphy’s and on Qantas BYO lists where somms want a pinot under $40 that still tastes like place—not like oak. Collectors ignore it; savvy suburban looking for Tuesday night acid fix buy by the six-pack.",
  "insider_take": "Most drinkers want Great Southern Pinot to feel like Burgundy—this doesn’t, and that’s its virtue. Buy the 2011 for its snap-pea stalk and river-stone bite, drink it at 14 °C, and stop pretending every Pinot needs silk. If you need velvet, spend twice as much elsewhere.",

parsed.market_position: You’ll spot Omrah限时特价 shelves at Dan Murphy’s and on Qantas BYO lists where somms want a pinot under $40 that still tastes like place—not like oak. Collectors ignore it; savvy suburban looking for Tuesday night acid fix buy by the six-pack.
parsed.insider_take: Most drinkers want Great Southern Pinot to feel like Burgundy—this doesn’t, and that’s its virtue. Buy the 2011 for its snap-pea stalk and river-stone bite, drink it at 14 °C, and stop pretending every Pinot needs silk. If you need velvet, spend twice as much elsewhere.
